analysis.one_liner: Requires all gun and ammunition sales to go through federally licensed dealers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House Judiciary subcommittee with zero cosponsors and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for any person to buy or sell a firearm or ammunition except through a federally licensed dealer, closing the private-sale gap that today allows transactions without a background check. It also raises dealer licensing fees, requires dealers to report buyers who seem troubled or are buying for someone else, and mandates annual training. Violating the rule would carry a prison term of 15 to 25 years and a fine of $75,000 to $150,000.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, communities affected by gun violence would benefit, since every sale — including private ones between strangers met online or at gun shows — would run through a licensed dealer's background check. Law enforcement would also get a dedicated tip line and mandatory dealer reports about suspicious buyers.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any individual to sell or buy a firearm or ammunition except through a federally licensed dealer, with criminal penalties of 15 to 25 years and a $75,000-$150,000 fine [S2][S3].
Requires licensed dealers to report suspected signs of mental duress, suicidal or homicidal ideation, or straw purchases to the Attorney General and local law enforcement [S2][S3].
Directs the Attorney General to set up a toll-free number the public can call at any time to report illegal or suspicious behavior at dealers' premises [S2][S3].
Requires each licensed dealer to complete an Attorney General-certified annual training course of at least 40 classroom hours on identifying high-risk customers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private gun owners and casual sellers would bear the heaviest cost: any sale outside a licensed dealer would become a serious federal crime carrying 15 to 25 years in prison. Small licensed dealers would pay sharply higher fees — up from $200 for three years to $500 a year, rising to $1,000 a year in 2021 — plus annual training and reporting duties. Anyone buying a gun privately would face waiting on a dealer's paperwork.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private gun sellers and small dealers

drawbacks.text: The penalty is severe: a minimum of 15 years in prison for any private sale, including transfers between family members or neighbors, which critics would call wildly out of proportion [S3].

Raising the dealer license fee from $200 for three years to as much as $1,000 per year could push small rural dealers out of business, leaving fewer places where buyers can legally complete a sale [S3].
The duty to report buyers showing 'signs of mental duress' or behavior that merely 'alarms' the dealer is vague, inviting inconsistent reporting and chilling lawful purchases [S3].
Mandatory 40-hour annual training is a recurring cost and scheduling burden, especially for small one-person shops [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — closing the private-sale loophole so every buyer gets a background check — is popular gun-safety policy and would likely prevent some prohibited buyers from getting guns. But this version is a blunt instrument: a 15-to-25-year mandatory prison term for any private transfer is far harsher than mainstream background-check proposals, and the steep fee increases could shrink the very dealer network the bill depends on. A narrower penalty structure would have kept the benefit while cutting the harshest costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its crime subcommittee, and died there without a markup, a vote, or any cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee introduced the bill on July 26, 2019 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
On August 28, 2019 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, where no further action was taken before the Congress ended January 3, 2021 [S5].
No member of the House — from either party — cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private gun sellers and gun owners who want to trade without a dealer background check are better off, since the current rules allowing unlicensed private sales remain in place. Small dealers also avoided the sharply higher fees and annual training mandate.

for.name: Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and named it for the 2018 Santa Fe High School shooting victims; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a markup or the floor; after the subcommittee referral the bill saw no further action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape was never tested; the lone sponsor was a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would route every gun and ammunition sale through licensed dealers, making them the mandatory checkpoint for all purchases and sending them more business — but it would also raise their license fees as much as fivefold, add a 40-hour annual training requirement, and expose them to license suspension for reporting failures. Their role as gatekeeper runs alongside the bill's public-safety aim.

The fee increase from $200 per three years to $1,000 per year, plus annual training and posting requirements, would fall hardest on small shops, potentially reducing the number of places buyers can legally complete a transfer.
